svg.title: CG limits: forward, aft, and what happens outside
svg.desc: Side view of an airplane with the CG range between the forward limit and the aft limit, which the manufacturer sets and publishes in the TCDS and the AFM or POH. In the PHAK worked example the range is 78 to 86 inches from the datum. A CG too far forward is nose heavy: hard to raise the nose at takeoff and landing, high nosewheel load, higher stall speed, higher control forces, and possibly impossible to flare. A CG too far aft is tail heavy: less stable, poorer recovery from stalls and spins, very light control forces that make overstress easy. If the CG is out of limits, relocate baggage, cargo or passengers before flight.
svg.text: CG limits: forward, aft, and what happens outside
Schematic side view. Limits are published in the TCDS and the AFM/POH. The 78 and 86 inch limits are
the PHAK worked example.

The CG is not fixed: it moves as variable load items are shifted or used up.
CG too far forward: nose heavy
Harder to control and raise the nose, especially
at takeoff and landing
Landing: excessive nosewheel load, nose-over
tendency on tailwheel airplanes, higher stall
speed, higher control forces
Extreme: difficult or impossible to flare for
landing
The forward limit also keeps enough elevator
deflection available at minimum airspeed
CG too far aft: tail heavy
Less stable: reduced ability to right itself
after maneuvering or turbulence
Reduces the capability to recover from stalls and
spins
Very light control forces make it easy to
overstress the aircraft
Extreme: control difficulty and violent stall
characteristics
Limits can vary with gross weight, and change for some operations such as acrobatic flight or gear
retraction
CG outside limits after loading: relocate items before flight. Baggage, cargo and seat assignment
control the CG; if tail heavy, put heavy passengers in forward seats
The CG is usually kept slightly forward of the center of lift: a nose-down tendency, desirable at high
AOA and slow speeds
